corrections.caveats: Baseline is the package's own pure-Go code (purego build tag), not C xxHash or any Go standard-library hash. The assembly is slower for 4-byte inputs (1.2 vs 1.3 GB/s) and the gain is about 1.2x at 16-100 B and 1.4x at 4 KB and above (derived from page data). Only amd64 numbers are published (Xeon Platinum 8252C); the arm64 assembly has no numbers. The README claim 'much faster than anything in the Go standard library' has no figures. Table last refreshed in the 2022-12-04 commit 'Update README for arm64 asm; latest benchmarks' with Go 1.19.2; newer Go compilers may narrow the gap. The benchmark discards Sum64's result, which is safe here because the assembly call cannot be eliminated and the pure-Go Sum64 is too large to inline.

notes: Numbers in claimed_speedup match the README table exactly. tier_reason: Peer-reviewed PLDI 2023 paper (checked-in PDF) states GCC 12.1.0 and Clang 15.0.6 with -march=native -mtune=native -O3, lists all ten CPU models (Table 1), fixed frequency/no boost/performance governor, and points to a public artifact with reproduction instructions (Zenodo DOI 10.5281/zenodo.7710435, not opened because zenodo is blocked) alongside the optimizer source in the repo; Table 4 and the abstract carry the claimed numbers.

corrections.stars_or_usage: 73 stars, 14 forks; PLDI 2023 Distinguished Paper Award and GECCO 2023 Humies Gold award (university news pages, snippet only); verified assembly published in fiat-crypto's fiat-amd64 directory and Curve25519 code integrated into BoringSSL (per the repo README)
corrections.caveats: The assembly is machine-generated by random program search, not hand-written; it sits here because it is compared against both compilers and hand-written assembly. Each platform's numbers come from code optimized on and for that same platform (best of three optimization runs per primitive per machine), against generic compiler output. Gains vary: Curve448 and P-521 multiply are slightly slower than GCC (0.98 and 0.97); gains are modest for Curve25519 and Poly1305. The baseline is Fiat Cryptography's generated C, not each library's own C. In whole scalar multiplication through SUPERCOP (Table 5, geometric-mean cycles) CryptOpt-enhanced code is on par with OpenSSL fe-51 (524k vs 530k) and fe-64 (461k vs 455k) assembly and slower than HACL* fe-64 (452k); for secp256k1, libsecp256k1's hand asm (547k) is itself slower than its portable C (530k), so CryptOpt's 527k (Fiat, verified) and 528k (Opt) are under 1 percent faster than libsecp256k1's C (derived from page data), and the 1.04 speedup over hand asm comes from the libsecp256k1-derived path that the equivalence checker cannot verify. The Zenodo artifact was not opened (blocked here); the repo README repeats the Table 4 means. Last commit 2023-11-16.

notes: Abstract (mean 1.74 over GCC 12.1.0, 1.40 over Clang 15.0.6, 1.04 over libsecp256k1 hand asm) and Table 4 multiply means match the record exactly. Metadata on github.com: Apache-2.0, 73 stars, 14 forks, not archived or a fork, default branch main, last commit 2023-11-16 (stale). Main shortcoming: whole-scalar-multiplication gains are within about 1 percent of existing hand asm or C, and two large fields are slightly slower than GCC.

tier_reason: First-party result.txt from the author's own harness (memcpy_bench.c, libs/*.asm) with the C flags in the Makefile and CPU models in the file, but no compiler, NASM or glibc version (the baseline is the prebuilt libc memcpy, so its version is the key unknown), no units in the file, and harness flaws (off-by-one average, timed first-touch page faults), so it falls short of A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: result.txt, seconds per copy of one 512 MiB buffer (MEM_ALLOC at the result commit; units from memcpy_bench.c's printf), lower is better. Xeon Platinum 8269CY: libc memcpy min 0.3494 / avg 0.3853 vs AVX-256 asm min 0.2711 / avg 0.2987 (about 1.29x), AVX-512 asm min 0.2854 / avg 0.3150 (about 1.22x), rep movsb min 0.3020 / avg 0.3333 (about 1.16x). AMD A8-6410: libc min 0.5464 / avg 0.6221 vs AVX asm min 0.4471 / avg 0.4967 (about 1.22-1.25x) and plain rep movsb min 0.4450 / avg 0.4970 (about 1.23-1.25x); AVX-512 not supported. Ratios derived from page data.
corrections.workload: Single-threaded copy of one large buffer per run (512 MiB when result.txt was recorded on 2020-09-20; the current code uses 128 MiB), 11 runs per routine; each run mallocs a fresh source (memset before timing) and a fresh, untouched destination, times one copy with gettimeofday, then checks it with memcmp. Routines: libc memcpy, NASM AVX-256 and AVX-512 unrolled copies with prefetcht1, and a three-instruction rep movsb. The multithreaded mode (option 5, libs/memcpy_multithread.c) was added later and is not in result.txt.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: gcc at the time of the results (Makefile switched to cc on 2020-09-21) with -Wall -ggdb3 -fPIC -fpic -O3 for the C harness; nasm -felf64 for the assembly; compiler, NASM and glibc versions not stated (the baseline memcpy is the prebuilt libc routine, so the C flags do not affect it)
corrections.hardware: AMD A8-6410 APU (2 GHz, no AVX-512) and Intel Xeon Platinum 8269CY (2.5 GHz; cpuinfo flags include 'hypervisor', so a cloud VM); README tells users to set the performance governor, not confirmed for these runs
corrections.caveats: Author's own runs; the README makes no speed claim. Harness flaws: the loop runs TEST_COUNT+1 = 11 copies but divides the total by 10, so every reported Avg exceeds its Max (Xeon libc Avg 0.3853 vs Max 0.3533); ratios survive because all routines share the bug. The destination is a fresh 512 MiB malloc (mmap) never touched before timing, so each timed copy includes about 131,072 first-touch page faults; derived copy rates of about 0.9-2.0 GB/s are well below memory bandwidth, so the numbers mix fault cost with copy speed and may reflect how each store pattern interacts with faulting rather than kernel efficiency. On the A8 the plain rep movsb routine matches the AVX routine, so the gain there is not from the AVX kernel. AVX-512 is slower than AVX-256 on the Xeon. glibc version (which selects the memcpy variant and its non-temporal threshold), compiler and NASM versions are unknown; one result set per machine. The current code uses a 128 MiB buffer, so rerunning it does not reproduce the recorded configuration. The asm measured equals today's libs/memcpy_avx256.asm (only a comment changed).

notes: Downgrade A to C: numbers match result.txt but the record's 'multithreaded harness' caveat and 'unit not stated' were wrong (single-threaded modes 1-4, seconds per 512 MiB copy); the harness averages 11 runs over 10 and times first-touch faults on a fresh destination. Metadata on github.com: Unlicense (public domain, OSI-approved, no patent grant), 13 stars, 2 forks, 24 commits, last commit 2020-09-22 (abandoned), not a fork. Shortcomings to record: no compiler/glibc versions, off-by-one Avg, page-fault-laden timing, rep movsb alone matches AVX on AMD, about 1.2-1.3x only.
